---
title: "Monorepos vs Polyrepos"
---

# Monorepos vs Polyrepos

After this page you can place `desk-web`, `desk-api`, and `desk-infra` in one Git repository or three, on purpose.

## Polyrepo (this book’s default so far)

Three repositories, three histories, three remotes:

```text
~/desk/desk-web
~/desk/desk-api
~/desk/desk-infra
```

Each clones, branches, and CI-runs on its own. A change that spans API and web is two pull requests. Versions of each other are documented (“web 1.2 needs api 1.4”) or ignored until something breaks.

## Monorepo

One repository:

```text
~/desk/desk/
  web/
  api/
  infra/
```

One `git clone`, one `main`, one PR can touch all three. CI must learn to run only what changed, or it becomes slow. Sparse checkout and partial clone (chapter 19) exist because monorepos grow.

## Trade-offs

| | Monorepo | Polyrepo |
|--|----------|----------|
| Cross-project change | One PR | Several PRs, several versions |
| Access control | One repo (paths, CODEOWNERS) | Separate remotes, easier per-team ACLs |
| CI | Must be smart or it is slow | Simple per repo |
| Submodules | Rarely needed | Common for shared libs |
| Git scale | Packfiles, sparse, LFS | Each repo stays small |

## Linux tooling

Path-based CI (`git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD | grep '^api/'`) is how a monorepo stays fast. `CODEOWNERS` (chapter 31) assigns `api/` to one team. None of that requires GitHub; the files are in Git.

## This book

Labs keep **three polyrepos** so platform chapters can push `desk-api` to GitLab and Forgejo independently. If your real desk is a monorepo, the Git commands are the same; only the directory layout changes. Worktrees still apply. Submodules usually do not.
